summary: S. 5221, titled the 'Stop Corrupt Trading Act', prohibits the President and Vice President, as well as related entities and other persons, from purchasing, selling, or exchanging nonpublic information obtained through official positions for financial benefit. The bill sets criminal penalties, prison terms, fines, criminal forfeiture, and civil enforcement actions managed by the Attorney General and the Office of Government Ethics.

affected_groups.effect: Prohibited from selling or exchanging nonpublic information gained from their official position for financial benefit, facing potential criminal and civil penalties for violations.

Entities controlled or partially owned by the President or Vice President, and any person knowingly providing value in a prohibited transaction, are prohibited from certain transactions and face joint and several liability for civil remedies.
Prohibited from acquiring, purchasing, selling, or exchanging nonpublic information for financial benefit, and subject to criminal and civil enforcement if they violate the prohibition.

key_provisions: Prohibits the President and Vice President (covered persons) and entities they control or own 5 percent or more of (covered entities) from selling or exchanging nonpublic information for financial benefit.
Prohibits any person from entering into a transaction to acquire, purchase, sell, or exchange nonpublic information for financial benefit.
Establishes criminal penalties including fines up to double the value of the transaction, imprisonment for up to 5 years, or both, alongside mandatory criminal forfeiture.
Grants authority to the Attorney General to bring civil actions for disgorgement, civil penalties up to the greater of $250,000 or three times the gain, and equitable relief.
Makes counterparties and covered entities jointly and severally liable for civil remedies if they knowingly provide anything of value in a prohibited transaction.
Requires the Director of the Office of Government Ethics to refer credible evidence of violations to the Attorney General and notify congressional judiciary committees.
